q: The living cells of cartilage, which lie in small spaces called lacunae within the matrix, are called:
x: Mature cartilage cells are chondrocytes, each sitting in a lacuna in the matrix. Osteocytes also lie in lacunae, but they are bone cells, not cartilage cells.

q: The C-shaped rings that keep the trachea open are made of:
x: The tracheal rings are hyaline cartilage, which is firm yet slightly flexible. Elastic cartilage supports the pinna and epiglottis, and fibrocartilage forms the intervertebral discs.

q: The external ear (pinna) can be bent and returns to its shape. It is supported by:
x: The pinna is supported by elastic cartilage, whose matrix has many yellow elastic fibres that give it flexibility and springiness. Hyaline cartilage is stiffer and has no network of elastic fibres.

q: The intervertebral discs between the bodies of adjacent vertebrae are made mainly of:
x: Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilage, whose matrix is packed with thick bundles of collagen fibres. This makes them tough enough to withstand the compression of the spine.

q: The epiglottis can bend and spring back to its shape because its cartilage matrix contains many:
x: The epiglottis is elastic cartilage; its yellow elastic fibres let it bend and recoil. Calcium phosphate crystals and Haversian canals are features of bone, not cartilage.

q: Under an ordinary light microscope, the matrix of hyaline cartilage looks clear and glassy because:
o: It contains no protein at all
It is heavily mineralised with calcium salts
It is packed with thick elastic fibres
Its fine collagen fibres are not visible in the matrix
x: Hyaline ('glass-like') cartilage does contain collagen, but the fibres are so fine that the matrix looks uniform and glassy. Thick, visible fibres are seen in fibrocartilage (collagen) and elastic cartilage (elastic fibres).

q: The layer of dense connective tissue that surrounds most hyaline and elastic cartilage is the:
x: Cartilage is covered by the perichondrium, which carries blood vessels and gives rise to new cartilage cells. The periosteum is the equivalent covering of bone.

q: The chondrocytes of cartilage obtain their oxygen and nutrients mainly by:
o: Capillaries running through canals in the matrix
Blood vessels in central Haversian canals
Red marrow present between the cells
Diffusion through the matrix from vessels around the cartilage
x: Cartilage has no blood vessels in its matrix, so substances diffuse through the matrix from vessels in the surrounding perichondrium. Haversian canals with blood vessels are found in compact bone.

q: Injured cartilage repairs much more slowly than injured bone. The main reason is that cartilage:
o: Has a matrix hardened by calcium salts
Is made only of elastic fibres
Has no blood vessels in its matrix
x: Cartilage is avascular: nutrients and repair cells reach it only slowly by diffusion, so healing is slow. It does contain living cells (chondrocytes), and its matrix is not mineralised like bone.

q: The bone cells that secrete new bone matrix are called:
x: Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells; they lay down the collagen and help deposit the mineral of new matrix. Osteoclasts do the opposite and break bone down.

q: Large, multinucleate cells that dissolve and resorb bone matrix are called:
x: Osteoclasts are large cells with many nuclei that break down bone matrix, releasing calcium and phosphate. Osteoblasts build bone and osteocytes maintain it.

q: An osteoblast that becomes surrounded by the matrix it has secreted, and stays in a lacuna, becomes a:
x: Once trapped in its own matrix, an osteoblast stops forming bone and becomes an osteocyte, a mature cell that maintains the surrounding matrix. Osteoclasts come from a different cell line and resorb bone.

q: In compact bone, the central canal of each osteon that carries blood vessels and nerves is the:
x: Each osteon (Haversian system) has a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels and nerves. Canaliculi are tiny channels between lacunae, and the medullary cavity is the large marrow space of the shaft.

q: In compact bone, the fine channels that connect neighbouring lacunae with each other and with the central canal are called:
x: Canaliculi are minute channels holding the cell processes of osteocytes, linking lacunae so that nutrients and wastes can pass. Volkmann's canals are much larger and link Haversian canals to each other.

q: Volkmann's canals in compact bone are canals that:
o: Run along the centre of each osteon
Run across the bone, linking Haversian canals with each other and the surface
x: Volkmann's canals run across (perpendicular or oblique to) the long axis of the bone and connect Haversian canals with each other and with the periosteum. The Haversian canal is the one along the centre of each osteon.

q: The basic structural unit of compact bone is the:
x: Compact bone is built of osteons: concentric lamellae of matrix around a central Haversian canal, with osteocytes in lacunae between them. Trabeculae are the bony struts of spongy bone.

q: Spongy (cancellous) bone is made of:
o: Closely packed osteons with no spaces
A network of thin bony bars and plates with spaces between them
Cartilage cells in a glassy matrix
x: Spongy bone is a lattice of thin bony bars and plates called trabeculae; the spaces between them hold red marrow. Closely packed osteons describe compact bone.

q: In a long bone such as the femur, spongy bone is found mainly in the:
x: The epiphyses (ends) of long bones are filled with spongy bone covered by a thin shell of compact bone. The wall of the shaft (diaphysis) is thick compact bone.

q: Which statement about compact bone is correct?
o: Its spaces between trabeculae are filled with red marrow
Its matrix lies in concentric lamellae around Haversian canals
It is found only at the ends of long bones
x: Compact bone is arranged as osteons, with matrix in concentric lamellae around Haversian canals and living osteocytes in lacunae. Trabeculae with red marrow describe spongy bone.

q: The tough fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of a bone, except over its joint surfaces, is the:
x: The periosteum covers bone except where articular cartilage lies; it carries vessels and bone-forming cells and anchors tendons. The endosteum lines the marrow cavity, and the perichondrium covers cartilage.

q: The main protein fibres present in the organic part of bone matrix are:
x: The organic part of bone matrix is mostly collagen fibres, which give bone tensile strength and slight flexibility. Elastin is typical of elastic cartilage, keratin of skin and hair, and actin of muscle.

q: The main mineral salt that makes bone hard is:
x: Bone hardness comes mainly from calcium phosphate (in the form of hydroxyapatite crystals) deposited on the collagen fibres. Calcium oxalate is the salt of some kidney stones, not of bone.

q: A chicken bone is left in dilute acid for several days. It becomes so flexible that it can be bent into a knot. This is because the acid has removed:
o: The mineral salts, leaving the collagen fibres
The collagen fibres, leaving the minerals
The bone cells, leaving the matrix unchanged
The marrow, leaving the compact bone unchanged
x: Acid dissolves the calcium phosphate, so only the flexible organic collagen framework is left. This shows that minerals give bone its hardness while collagen gives it flexibility.

q: A bone that is strongly heated until all organic matter burns away keeps its shape but becomes very brittle. This shows that the organic collagen of bone mainly provides:
x: Burning removes the collagen and leaves only the minerals, so the bone is still hard but crumbles easily. Collagen therefore gives bone its toughness and slight flexibility, while minerals give hardness and store calcium.

q: A single skeletal muscle cell, which is long and cylindrical, is called a:
x: Each skeletal muscle cell is called a muscle fibre. Myofibrils are the thread-like structures inside a fibre, and sarcomeres and myofilaments are smaller units within the myofibrils.

q: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by:
x: Tendons are cords of dense collagen-rich connective tissue that join muscle to bone and transmit the pull of contraction. Ligaments join bone to bone at joints.

q: Ligaments differ from tendons in that ligaments:
o: Join bones to other bones at joints
x: Ligaments connect bone to bone and hold joints together; they are somewhat more elastic than tendons. Tendons connect muscle to bone.

q: The firm but flexible matrix of cartilage, secreted by its cells, is called:
x: Cartilage matrix is a firm, rubbery material called chondrin, with fibres embedded in it. Hydroxyapatite is the calcium phosphate mineral of bone.

q: Young, actively dividing cells that produce new cartilage matrix are called:
x: Chondroblasts secrete cartilage matrix; once enclosed in lacunae they become chondrocytes. Osteoblasts are the matrix-forming cells of bone, not cartilage.

q: Which feature is found in BOTH cartilage and bone?
o: A matrix hardened by calcium phosphate
Cells lying in lacunae within a matrix
x: In both tissues the cells (chondrocytes or osteocytes) lie in lacunae surrounded by matrix. Mineralised matrix and Haversian canals with blood vessels belong to bone only; cartilage matrix has no vessels.

q: Which type of cartilage has no perichondrium covering it?
o: Hyaline cartilage of the tracheal rings
x: Fibrocartilage lacks a perichondrium; it merges with surrounding dense connective tissue. Hyaline cartilage of the trachea and elastic cartilage of the ear and epiglottis are covered by perichondrium.

q: Fibrocartilage is the toughest type of cartilage because its matrix contains:
x: Fibrocartilage has dense bundles of collagen fibres in its matrix, so it resists both compression and pulling. Yellow elastic fibres give flexibility to elastic cartilage instead.

q: The skeleton of an adult human normally consists of:
x: The adult human skeleton normally has 206 bones. A newborn has more separate bony pieces, which fuse during growth to give the adult number.

q: Red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are produced in the:
x: Red bone marrow is the site of blood cell formation (haemopoiesis). Yellow marrow is mainly fat, and the periosteum and cartilage do not make blood cells.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the human skeleton?
x: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, provides levers for movement, stores minerals and makes blood cells. Digestive enzymes are made by glands of the digestive system, not by bone.

q: Bones act as the body's main reservoir of which minerals?
x: Bone matrix stores large amounts of calcium and phosphate, which can be released into the blood when needed. Sodium and potassium are mainly in body fluids, and iodine is concentrated in the thyroid.

q: Which pairing of a skeletal structure with the organ it protects is correct?
x: The vertebral column encloses and protects the spinal cord. The cranium protects the brain, and the rib cage protects the heart and lungs.

q: In producing movement, the role of the bones is to act as:
x: Bones act as rigid levers that are pulled by contracting muscles; the joints act as the fulcrums. The force (effort) comes from the muscles, not the bones.

q: Which group of bones belongs entirely to the axial skeleton?
o: Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum
x: The axial skeleton forms the central axis: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum. The clavicle and scapula belong to the pectoral girdle, which is part of the appendicular skeleton.

q: Which bone is part of the appendicular skeleton?
x: The scapula belongs to the pectoral girdle, part of the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles). The sternum, sacrum and hyoid all belong to the axial skeleton.

q: Each half of the pectoral (shoulder) girdle consists of the:
x: Each side of the pectoral girdle is formed by the clavicle (collarbone) and scapula (shoulder blade). The humerus is a limb bone that joins the girdle, and the ilium, ischium and pubis form the hip bone.

q: Each hip bone of the pelvic girdle is formed by the fusion of three bones. These are the:
x: Each hip bone forms from the fused ilium, ischium and pubis. The sacrum and coccyx are part of the vertebral column (axial skeleton), and the femur is the thigh bone.

q: The longest and strongest bone in the human body is the:
x: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone. The tibia and fibula are in the lower leg, and the humerus is in the upper arm.

q: The two bones of the human forearm are the:
x: The forearm contains the radius and ulna. The humerus is the single bone of the upper arm, and the tibia and fibula are the bones of the lower leg.

q: The patella (kneecap) is a bone that:
o: Forms part of the pelvic girdle
Joins the tibia to the fibula
Develops within a tendon in front of the knee joint
x: The patella is a sesamoid bone that forms inside the tendon of the thigh muscle in front of the knee. It is part of the appendicular skeleton (lower limb), not the girdle or axial skeleton.

q: Which is the correct order of the regions of the vertebral column, from the neck downwards?
x: From top to bottom the vertebral column has cervical (neck), thoracic (chest), lumbar (lower back), sacral and coccygeal regions. The thoracic vertebrae carry the ribs.

q: At the back, the ribs articulate with the:
x: The ribs join the thoracic vertebrae at the back. Cervical vertebrae are in the neck, and lumbar vertebrae of the lower back carry no ribs.

q: The number of cervical (neck) vertebrae in humans is:
x: Humans have seven cervical vertebrae. Twelve is the number of thoracic vertebrae, and five is the number of lumbar vertebrae.

q: The last two pairs of ribs are called floating ribs because they:
o: Are not attached to the vertebrae
Have no attachment to the sternum at the front
x: Floating ribs are attached to thoracic vertebrae at the back but have no connection to the sternum at the front. They are still bony ribs held in the body wall.

q: The hyaline costal cartilages that join the ribs to the sternum help breathing by:
o: Giving the rib cage flexibility to move
Keeping the rib cage completely rigid
x: Costal cartilages are firm but flexible, so the rib cage can expand and recoil during breathing. A completely rigid chest could not change its volume.

q: The layer of hyaline cartilage covering the ends of bones at movable joints mainly:
x: Articular cartilage gives a smooth, slippery surface that reduces friction and cushions the bones. Synovial fluid is produced by the synovial membrane, not by the cartilage.

q: The fibrocartilage discs between vertebrae mainly serve to:
o: Produce blood cells for the body
Attach the ribs to the vertebrae
Absorb shocks and allow slight bending of the spine
Store fat in the vertebral column
x: Intervertebral discs act as cushions that absorb shocks during walking and jumping, and they allow limited bending and twisting of the spine. They do not make blood cells or store fat.

q: In the human embryo, most of the bones of the skeleton are first formed as models made of:
x: Most of the embryonic skeleton is first laid down as hyaline cartilage, which is gradually replaced by bone (ossification). Elastic and fibrocartilage are found only at particular sites.

q: During childhood, a long bone grows in length mainly at the:
o: Plate of cartilage between the shaft and each end
Articular cartilage at the joint surface
x: A plate of hyaline cartilage (growth or epiphyseal plate) between the shaft and each end keeps growing and being replaced by bone, lengthening the bone. The periosteum adds bone to the outside, increasing thickness rather than length.

q: Bone is constantly remodelled throughout life. This depends on the balanced activity of:
o: Osteoblasts depositing bone and osteoclasts resorbing it
x: Bone is living tissue: osteoblasts lay down new matrix while osteoclasts break down old matrix. The balance between them shapes and repairs bone throughout life.

q: In an elderly person, osteoclast activity exceeds osteoblast activity for many years. The most direct result is that the bones:
o: Take up calcium from the blood
Become less dense and fracture more easily
x: If resorption by osteoclasts is greater than deposition by osteoblasts, bone mass falls and bones become porous and fragile. Resorption releases calcium into the blood rather than taking it up.

q: When the calcium level of the blood falls, calcium is released from bone into the blood mainly by the activity of:
x: Osteoclasts dissolve bone matrix and release its calcium and phosphate into the blood. Osteoblasts do the reverse, using calcium to build new matrix.

q: Cartilage differs from bone in that cartilage:
o: Has a matrix hardened by calcium phosphate
Is flexible and has no blood vessels in its matrix
x: Cartilage is flexible and avascular, its cells fed by diffusion. Periosteum, Haversian systems and a calcium-phosphate-hardened matrix are features of bone.

q: Spongy bone at the ends of long bones is useful because it:
o: Forms a dense outer tube that resists bending
Is the main site of fat storage in adults
Makes the bone lighter while staying strong, and holds red marrow
x: The trabeculae of spongy bone give strength with less weight, and their spaces hold red marrow. The dense outer tube of the shaft is compact bone, and adult fat storage is in yellow marrow.

q: In an adult, red bone marrow is found mainly in the:
o: Medullary cavity of the shafts of long bones
Spongy bone of flat bones such as the sternum, ribs and hip bones
Compact bone of the shaft wall
x: In adults, red marrow is mostly in the spongy bone of flat and irregular bones (sternum, ribs, hip bones, vertebrae) and the ends of some long bones. The shaft cavity of adult long bones holds yellow marrow.

q: Which skull bone forms the movable lower jaw?
x: The mandible is the lower jaw bone and moves at its joint with the temporal bone during chewing and speaking. The maxilla is the upper jaw, which is fixed to the rest of the skull.

q: The hyoid bone in the neck is classified as part of the:
x: The hyoid lies along the body's central axis and is grouped with the axial skeleton (skull, hyoid, vertebral column, ribs and sternum). The girdles and limbs form the appendicular skeleton.

q: Compared with the pectoral girdle, the pelvic girdle is:
o: Firmly joined to the vertebral column, giving stability for bearing weight
More loosely attached, giving the limb a greater range of movement
Made of the clavicle and scapula
x: The hip bones are firmly joined to the sacrum, giving a stable base to carry body weight. The pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula) is loosely attached, which gives the arm its wide range of movement.

q: Which statement correctly compares red and yellow bone marrow?
o: Yellow marrow forms blood cells, while red marrow mainly stores fat
Red marrow is found only in the shaft cavity of adult long bones
Red marrow forms blood cells, while yellow marrow mainly stores fat
Yellow marrow is found only in children
x: Red marrow is the blood-forming tissue, while yellow marrow is mostly fat. In adults the shaft cavities of long bones hold yellow marrow, and much red marrow of childhood is replaced by yellow marrow with age.

q: Intercalated discs are found in:
x: Intercalated discs are specialised junctions joining cardiac muscle cells end to end. They are absent from skeletal and smooth muscle.

q: Which type of muscle shows NO cross-striations?
x: Smooth muscle is non-striated (unstriped). Skeletal and cardiac muscle are both striated; the tongue is made of skeletal muscle.

q: Which description fits a skeletal muscle fibre?
o: Short, branched and with one central nucleus
Spindle-shaped, unstriated, with one central nucleus
Branched, striated and joined by intercalated discs
x: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, cylindrical, unbranched cells with many nuclei. Spindle-shaped cells describe smooth muscle, and branched cells with intercalated discs describe cardiac muscle.

q: Smooth muscle cells are:
o: Spindle-shaped with a single central nucleus
x: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (tapering at both ends), each with one centrally placed nucleus. Many peripheral nuclei are a feature of skeletal muscle.

q: Cardiac muscle cells are:
o: Branched, striated, with one or two central nuclei
x: Cardiac muscle cells are striated and branched, usually with one (sometimes two) centrally placed nuclei. Unbranched multinucleate fibres are skeletal muscle.

q: Which type of muscle is under conscious (voluntary) control?
x: Skeletal muscle is voluntary: we can contract it at will. Cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary and controlled by the autonomic nervous system and hormones.

q: Smooth muscle is found in the:
x: Smooth muscle lines hollow organs such as the urinary bladder, gut, uterus and blood vessels. The biceps and eye-moving muscles are skeletal, and the heart wall is cardiac muscle.

q: The diaphragm, which contracts during breathing even while we sleep, is made of:
x: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle supplied by motor nerves; we can also control breathing voluntarily. Its automatic rhythm comes from the brain's breathing centre, not from smooth or cardiac muscle.

q: The intercalated discs of cardiac muscle are important because they:
o: Let impulses pass quickly from cell to cell so the muscle contracts as a unit
Separate the heart wall into thin layers
x: Intercalated discs hold cardiac cells firmly together and contain gap junctions that let the impulse spread rapidly, so the heart muscle contracts in a coordinated way. They have nothing to do with voluntary control.

q: The cross-striations seen in skeletal and cardiac muscle are due to:
o: The regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments
Bands of connective tissue around each fibre
x: Striations are alternating light and dark bands formed by the orderly arrangement of thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments in sarcomeres. Intercalated discs occur only in cardiac muscle and are not the source of the striations.

q: Smooth muscle contains actin and myosin, yet it shows no striations. This is because in smooth muscle:
o: Actin and myosin are present only in the nucleus
The cells are joined by intercalated discs
The filaments are not arranged in regular repeating sarcomeres
x: Smooth muscle has actin and myosin, but they are not lined up in regular sarcomeres, so no bands are seen. Striations appear only when the filaments are arranged in an orderly repeating pattern.

q: The autonomic nerves supplying the heart:
o: Alter the rate and force of the heartbeat but do not start it
Make cardiac muscle a voluntary muscle
Are the only reason cardiac muscle is striated
x: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: each beat starts in the heart's own pacemaker. Autonomic nerves only speed up or slow down the rate and change the force of contraction.

q: Which muscle is striated AND contracts rhythmically throughout life without fatigue?
x: Cardiac muscle is striated and beats non-stop throughout life without tiring. Skeletal muscle is striated but fatigues, and smooth muscle is not striated.

q: Compared with skeletal muscle, smooth muscle contracts:
o: Only when we consciously decide to
Slowly, and can keep up its contraction for a long time
With exactly the same speed as skeletal muscle
x: Smooth muscle contracts slowly but can sustain contraction for long periods, as in the walls of blood vessels and the gut. Rapid, quickly tiring contraction is typical of skeletal muscle.

q: Contraction of the smooth muscle in the wall of the intestine is controlled mainly by:
o: Somatic motor nerves under conscious control
x: Smooth muscle of the gut is involuntary and controlled by the autonomic nervous system (and some hormones). Somatic motor nerves supply skeletal muscle.

q: In which muscle do many nuclei lie at the edge of each fibre, just beneath the cell membrane?
x: Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleate with nuclei placed peripherally under the sarcolemma. Smooth and cardiac muscle cells have central nuclei; the iris muscles are smooth.

q: A tissue sample shows striated, branched cells, each with a central nucleus, joined end to end by dark transverse bands. The sample was most probably taken from the:
x: Branched, striated cells with central nuclei and dark bands (intercalated discs) are cardiac muscle, found in the heart wall. Stomach and artery walls contain smooth muscle, and thigh muscle is skeletal.

q: A tissue sample shows unbranched, spindle-shaped cells without striations, each with one central nucleus. This tissue could have come from the:
x: These are smooth muscle cells, which form the wall of the uterus (and other hollow organs). The tongue and biceps are skeletal muscle, and the heart wall is cardiac muscle.

q: The muscles of the iris that change the size of the pupil are:
x: The iris muscles are smooth muscles controlled by the autonomic nervous system, so pupil size changes automatically with light. They are not under voluntary control.

q: Which feature is shared by cardiac and skeletal muscle but absent from smooth muscle?
x: Both cardiac and skeletal muscle are striated, while smooth muscle is not. Intercalated discs are only in cardiac muscle, and voluntary control and peripheral nuclei are only in skeletal muscle.

q: Cardiac muscle and smooth muscle are alike in being:
x: Both cardiac and smooth muscle are involuntary, working without conscious control. Only cardiac muscle is striated and branched, and neither is multinucleate like skeletal muscle.

q: Which statement about skeletal muscle is NOT correct?
o: It is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
It is attached to bones by tendons
x: Skeletal muscle is supplied by somatic motor nerves and is under voluntary control; the autonomic system controls cardiac and smooth muscle. The other statements are true of skeletal muscle.

q: Smooth muscle is also called visceral muscle because it:
o: Is found in the walls of internal organs
Is found only in the heart
x: 'Visceral' refers to the internal organs (viscera); smooth muscle forms the walls of the gut, bladder, uterus and blood vessels. Muscle attached to the skeleton is skeletal muscle.

q: Which pair of terms correctly describes skeletal muscle?
x: Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, and smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary.

q: Waves of peristalsis that move food along the small intestine are produced by:
o: Smooth muscle in the intestinal wall
Skeletal muscle in the abdominal wall
x: Peristalsis is caused by slow, rhythmic contractions of smooth muscle layers in the gut wall. Abdominal skeletal muscle does not move food along the intestine.

q: Which set of features is entirely correct for cardiac muscle?
o: Striated, voluntary, branched, with intercalated discs
Striated, involuntary, branched, with intercalated discs
Non-striated, involuntary, branched, with intercalated discs
x: Cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary, branched and joined by intercalated discs. Each other set has one wrong feature: voluntary, non-striated, or unbranched and multinucleate.

q: A heart removed from the body and kept in a suitable salt solution continues to beat for some time. This shows that cardiac muscle is:
x: Cardiac muscle is myogenic: its contraction starts within the muscle itself (the pacemaker), so it beats even without nerve connections. A neurogenic heart would need nerve impulses to beat.

q: The muscles that move the tongue during speech and chewing are:
x: The tongue is made of skeletal muscle, which is why we can move it voluntarily and quickly. Smooth (visceral) muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs.

q: During childbirth, the hormone oxytocin causes strong contractions of the:
o: Smooth muscle of the uterine wall
x: Oxytocin stimulates contraction of the smooth muscle in the uterus wall during labour. This shows that smooth muscle can be controlled by hormones as well as by autonomic nerves.

q: Which pair is correctly matched?
x: Intercalated discs are a feature of cardiac muscle. Peripheral nuclei belong to skeletal muscle, spindle-shaped cells to smooth muscle, and cardiac muscle is involuntary.

q: A poison blocks transmission from somatic motor nerves to the muscles they supply. Which muscle would stop contracting?
x: Somatic motor nerves supply only skeletal muscle, so the limb muscles would be paralysed. The heart is myogenic, and smooth muscle of the gut and iris is controlled by autonomic nerves.

q: The functional contractile unit of a myofibril in skeletal muscle is the:
x: The sarcomere is the repeating contractile unit of a myofibril. The sarcolemma is the cell membrane, the sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium ions.

q: A sarcomere is the part of a myofibril lying between two successive:
x: Each sarcomere runs from one Z line to the next. The M line and H zone lie in the middle of the sarcomere, not at its ends.

q: The cell membrane of a skeletal muscle fibre is called the:
x: The plasma membrane of a muscle fibre is the sarcolemma. The neurilemma surrounds nerve fibres and the tonoplast surrounds a plant cell vacuole.

q: The dark band of a sarcomere, which spans the whole length of the thick filaments, is the:
x: The A (anisotropic) band is dark and equals the length of the thick myosin filaments. The H zone is only the lighter central part of the A band, and the I band is the light band.

q: In a relaxed sarcomere, the I band contains:
o: The M line and thick filaments
x: The light I band is the region where only thin actin filaments are present, on either side of a Z line. Thick filaments are confined to the A band.

q: A thin cross-section is cut through the H zone of a relaxed sarcomere. It would show:
o: Neither filament, only Z line protein
x: The H zone is the central part of the A band that thin filaments do not reach in a relaxed fibre, so a section there shows only myosin. A section through the outer A band would show both filaments.

q: The Z line lies in the middle of which band or zone?
o: Overlap region of the A band
x: Each Z line bisects an I band, so half of each I band belongs to one sarcomere and half to the next. The M line, not the Z line, lies in the middle of the A band and H zone.

q: The thick filaments of skeletal muscle are made mainly of the protein:
x: Thick filaments are made of myosin molecules. Actin, troponin and tropomyosin are the proteins of the thin filaments.

q: The thin filaments of a skeletal muscle sarcomere are made of:
x: A thin filament is a helix of actin with the regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin attached. Myosin forms the thick filaments, and myoglobin is an oxygen-storing pigment in the sarcoplasm.

q: Which part of a myosin molecule binds to actin and has ATPase activity?
x: The globular myosin heads bind actin and split ATP, so they act as ATPase. The tail forms the shaft of the thick filament; tropomyosin and troponin belong to the thin filament.

q: In a resting skeletal muscle fibre, the myosin-binding sites on actin are covered by:
x: In resting muscle the strands of tropomyosin lie over the binding sites on actin, so myosin heads cannot attach. Troponin holds tropomyosin in this blocking position until calcium ions bind to troponin.

q: Which protein of the thin filament binds calcium ions?
x: Troponin is the calcium-binding protein of the thin filament. Tropomyosin covers the binding sites but does not itself bind calcium.

q: The main role of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in a skeletal muscle fibre is to:
o: Store glycogen as an energy reserve
Carry the impulse from the surface into the fibre
Store calcium ions and release them on stimulation
x: The sarcoplasmic reticulum, a modified smooth ER, stores Ca²⁺ and releases it when the fibre is stimulated. Carrying the impulse inward is the job of the T-tubules, and ATP is made in mitochondria.

q: Transverse tubules (T-tubules) of a skeletal muscle fibre are:
o: Sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum that store calcium ions
Bundles of thin filaments attached to the Z line
Channels inside mitochondria that make ATP
Inward folds of the sarcolemma that carry the impulse deep into the fibre
x: T-tubules are tube-like inward extensions of the sarcolemma. They carry the action potential from the surface into the interior of the fibre, close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

q: In a skeletal muscle fibre, the nuclei are:
o: One, lying in the centre of the cell
Two, lying in the centre of the cell
Many, lying just beneath the sarcolemma
x: A skeletal muscle fibre is a long cell with many nuclei placed at the edge, just under the sarcolemma. A single central nucleus is a feature of smooth and cardiac muscle cells.

q: Which pigment in the sarcoplasm of muscle fibres binds and stores oxygen?
x: Myoglobin is the red, oxygen-storing pigment of muscle fibres. Haemoglobin carries oxygen inside red blood cells, not in muscle sarcoplasm.

q: The cross-striations of skeletal muscle are caused by:
o: Rows of nuclei arranged across the fibre
Alternating dark A bands and light I bands lined up across myofibrils
x: The A and I bands of neighbouring myofibrils are lined up, giving the fibre its dark and light striations. Intercalated discs are found in cardiac muscle, not skeletal muscle.

q: Myofibrils inside a skeletal muscle fibre are made of:
x: Each myofibril is built of thin actin and thick myosin myofilaments arranged in sarcomeres. Muscle fibres are whole cells, which are larger than myofibrils.

q: Which is the correct order from the largest to the smallest structure in a skeletal muscle?
o: Muscle → muscle fibre → bundle of fibres → myofilament → myofibril
Muscle → myofibril → muscle fibre → bundle of fibres → myofilament
Muscle → bundle of fibres → myofibril → muscle fibre → myofilament
Muscle → bundle of fibres → muscle fibre → myofibril → myofilament
x: A muscle is made of bundles of muscle fibres (cells). Each fibre contains many myofibrils, and each myofibril is made of actin and myosin myofilaments.

q: In a relaxed sarcomere, where are both thick and thin filaments present together?
o: In the parts of the A band on either side of the H zone
x: Thin filaments extend from the Z lines into the outer parts of the A band, where they overlap the thick filaments. The H zone has thick filaments only and the I band has thin filaments only.

q: The thick filaments of a sarcomere are linked to one another at their centres by the:
x: The M line runs through the centre of the A band and holds the thick filaments in place. Thin filaments, by contrast, are anchored at the Z lines.

q: Each thin filament consists of:
o: Two chains of globular actin twisted into a helix, with regulatory proteins
A single straight chain of myosin heads
A bundle of myosin tails with two heads each
A coiled strand of collagen fibres
x: Thin filaments are made of two chains of globular actin molecules twisted round each other, with tropomyosin and troponin attached. Heads and tails describe myosin, the thick filament.

q: Which pair of proteins acts as regulatory proteins, controlling when contraction can occur?
x: Troponin and tropomyosin control whether actin's binding sites are open to myosin. Actin and myosin are the contractile proteins that actually slide and pull.

q: A single myosin molecule consists of:
o: A long tail with two globular heads
Two chains of globular subunits twisted together
A ring of protein around the Z line
x: Each myosin molecule has a long rod-like tail and two globular heads. Many molecules bundle by their tails to form a thick filament, with the heads sticking out.

q: The cross-bridges seen between filaments in skeletal muscle are formed by:
o: Troponin molecules on the thin filaments
Myosin heads projecting from the thick filaments
x: The myosin heads stick out from the thick filaments and attach to actin, forming cross-bridges. Troponin is a regulatory protein and does not form the bridge itself.

q: T-tubules lie close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This arrangement allows:
o: ATP to flow from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the T-tubules
Myoglobin to pass oxygen into the T-tubules
New actin filaments to be made between the tubules
An impulse at the surface to trigger Ca²⁺ release deep inside the fibre at once
x: Because T-tubules carry the action potential inward right next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium is released throughout the fibre almost at the same time. This lets all myofibrils contract together.

q: In skeletal muscle, the term 'muscle fibre' refers to:
o: A bundle of many muscle cells
x: A skeletal muscle fibre is one long cylindrical cell containing many nuclei. Bundles of fibres make up the muscle, and protein filaments lie inside the fibre.

q: Moving from a Z line to the centre of a relaxed sarcomere, which order of regions is met?
o: H zone → I band → overlap part of A band → M line
Half of I band → overlap part of A band → H zone → M line
Overlap part of A band → half of I band → H zone → M line
Half of I band → H zone → overlap part of A band → M line
x: From the Z line you first pass the thin-only I band, then the outer A band where thick and thin overlap, then the thick-only H zone, reaching the M line at the centre.

q: The main role of the many mitochondria lying between myofibrils in a muscle fibre is to:
o: Supply ATP for contraction and calcium pumping
Make the actin and myosin proteins
x: Mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration; ATP is needed by myosin heads and by the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Proteins are made on ribosomes, and calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

q: Which statement about the sarcoplasmic reticulum is NOT correct?
o: It is a specialised form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum
It forms a network of sacs around each myofibril
It stores Ca²⁺ in a resting fibre
It opens to the outside of the cell, carrying extracellular fluid inward
x: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a closed internal network of smooth ER around the myofibrils that stores calcium. It is the T-tubules, as inward folds of the sarcolemma, that open to the outside.

q: Which pairing of a sarcomere structure with its feature is correct?
o: M line — anchors the thin filaments at the centre
Z line — anchors the thin filaments at each end of the sarcomere
I band — contains thick filaments only
H zone — region where thick and thin filaments overlap
x: Thin actin filaments are attached to the Z lines. The M line links thick filaments, the I band holds thin filaments only, and the H zone has thick filaments only.

q: A myofibril is made of:
o: Many muscle fibres joined end to end
Many sarcomeres joined end to end
x: A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres repeated end to end along its length, which gives the regular banding. Muscle fibres and bundles are larger units that contain myofibrils.

q: The neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction of skeletal muscle is:
x: Motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which excites the skeletal muscle fibre. The other three are transmitters or hormones with other roles.

q: Which ions, released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, start skeletal muscle contraction?
x: Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin and starts contraction. Sodium and potassium ions are involved in the action potential, not in uncovering actin.

q: The model which explains muscle contraction as thin filaments moving past thick filaments is the:
x: The sliding filament theory states that actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, shortening the sarcomere. The other models explain membranes, ATP synthesis and enzyme action.

q: The molecule directly split by myosin heads to power contraction is:
x: Myosin heads hydrolyse ATP for the energy of the cross-bridge cycle. Creatine phosphate only helps to remake ATP, and glucose must first be respired.

q: Which part of the sarcomere keeps the same length during contraction?
x: The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, which do not shorten, so it stays the same. The I band, H zone and the sarcomere as a whole all shorten.

q: During contraction of a skeletal muscle fibre, the I band and the H zone:
o: I band shortens while the H zone lengthens
x: As thin filaments slide toward the centre, the thin-only I band and the thick-only H zone both narrow. Only the A band keeps its length.

q: According to the sliding filament theory, during contraction:
o: Both actin and myosin filaments shorten
Thick filaments slide outward toward the Z lines
Thin filaments slide inward over thick filaments toward the M line
Thin filaments slide away from the M line
x: The myosin heads pull the actin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere. Neither filament changes its own length; they simply overlap more.

q: When Ca²⁺ binds to troponin in a skeletal muscle fibre:
o: ATP is made by the myosin heads
Tropomyosin shifts and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin
x: Calcium binding changes the shape of troponin, which pulls tropomyosin away from the binding sites. Myosin heads can then attach to actin and form cross-bridges.

q: When a new ATP molecule binds to a myosin head that is attached to actin, the head:
x: Binding of ATP releases the myosin head from actin, breaking the cross-bridge. Without ATP the head stays locked on actin, as in rigor mortis.

q: After it detaches from actin, the myosin head hydrolyses ATP. This:
o: Makes the head detach from actin
Pumps sodium ions out of the fibre
Energises (cocks) the head ready to bind actin again
x: Splitting ATP into ADP and phosphate moves the head into its high-energy position, ready to form a new cross-bridge. Detachment was caused by ATP binding, not by its hydrolysis.

q: What happens during the power stroke of the cross-bridge cycle?
o: A new ATP binds and the myosin head lets go of actin
The myosin head pivots, pulling the thin filament toward the sarcomere centre
Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Acetylcholine is released from the nerve ending
x: In the power stroke the attached myosin head tilts and releases ADP and phosphate, dragging the actin filament toward the M line. ATP binding afterwards detaches the head.

q: Which sequence of events leads to contraction of a skeletal muscle fibre?
o: ACh released → sarcolemma depolarised → impulse along T-tubules → Ca²⁺ released → Ca²⁺ binds troponin → cross-bridges form
Ca²⁺ released → ACh released → T-tubules depolarised → cross-bridges form → Ca²⁺ binds troponin
Sarcolemma depolarised → ACh released → Ca²⁺ binds troponin → Ca²⁺ released → cross-bridges form
ACh released → Ca²⁺ binds troponin → impulse along T-tubules → cross-bridges form → Ca²⁺ released
x: Acetylcholine excites the sarcolemma, the impulse travels down the T-tubules, the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases calcium, calcium binds troponin, and only then can myosin attach to actin.

q: A skeletal muscle fibre relaxes when:
o: Ca²⁺ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The ATP in the fibre runs out
Ca²⁺ is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Acetylcholine stays bound to its receptors
x: Removing calcium lets tropomyosin cover actin again, so cross-bridges stop forming. Running out of ATP does not relax muscle; it locks the myosin heads in place.

q: The role of the enzyme acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction is to:
o: Make acetylcholine in the nerve ending
Pump Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Break down acetylcholine so the fibre is not kept stimulated
x: Acetylcholinesterase quickly breaks down acetylcholine in the cleft, ending each stimulus. Without it the muscle fibre would keep being excited.

q: Rigor mortis, the stiffening of muscles after death, occurs because:
o: Too much ATP builds up in the muscle
No ATP is made, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Lactic acid dissolves the thin filaments
x: After death ATP is no longer produced, and ATP is needed to release myosin heads from actin. The cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles become rigid.

q: The term 'oxygen debt' refers to:
o: The oxygen stored in myoglobin at rest
The extra oxygen taken in after vigorous exercise to remove accumulated lactic acid
The shortage of oxygen in the air at high altitude
The oxygen used by resting muscles each minute
x: During hard exercise muscles respire anaerobically and form lactic acid. Afterwards extra oxygen is breathed in to oxidise or convert this lactic acid; this extra amount is the oxygen debt.

q: When oxygen supply cannot keep up during vigorous exercise, skeletal muscle cells respire anaerobically, producing:
x: Anaerobic respiration in human muscle converts pyruvate into lactic acid. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products in yeast, and urea and uric acid are nitrogenous wastes.

q: During prolonged, vigorous exercise with too little oxygen, which substance builds up in the muscle and is linked with fatigue in the textbook account?
o: Accumulation of extra glycogen in the muscle
Accumulation of lactic acid in the muscle
Excess creatine phosphate in the fibre
x: When oxygen runs short, muscle respires anaerobically and lactic acid builds up; the textbook links this, together with falling energy reserves, to fatigue. Glycogen and creatine phosphate are used up, not built up, and oxygen is in short supply, not in excess.

q: The role of creatine phosphate in a working skeletal muscle is to:
o: Bind calcium ions released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Cover the binding sites on actin
x: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate to ADP, quickly remaking ATP during the first seconds of activity. Oxygen is stored by myoglobin and calcium binds troponin.

q: The junction between a motor neuron's axon terminal and a skeletal muscle fibre is the:
x: The neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in the myelin sheath, and intercalated discs join cardiac cells.

q: When acetylcholine binds to its receptors on the sarcolemma, the first effect is:
o: Depolarisation of the sarcolemma, starting an action potential
Pumping of Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Hydrolysis of ATP by myosin heads
x: Acetylcholine opens ion channels in the sarcolemma, which depolarises and fires an action potential. Calcium release and cross-bridge cycling follow later.

q: When an impulse reaches a motor neuron's terminal, acetylcholine is released into the cleft by:
o: Exocytosis of synaptic vesicles, triggered by Ca²⁺ entry
Osmosis of water from the terminal
x: The impulse opens calcium channels in the terminal; calcium entry makes vesicles fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine by exocytosis.

q: Which event is NOT part of the relaxation of a skeletal muscle fibre?
o: Pumping of Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Tropomyosin covering the binding sites on actin again
Release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
x: Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum starts contraction. Relaxation involves stopping the stimulus, pumping calcium back and re-covering actin's binding sites.

q: A motor unit consists of:
o: One muscle fibre and all its myofibrils
One sarcomere and its two Z lines
One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies
All the motor neurons supplying one muscle
x: A motor unit is a single motor neuron together with every muscle fibre its branches supply. When that neuron fires, all of its fibres contract together.

q: When a myosin head first attaches to actin to form a cross-bridge, it is carrying:
x: The cocked head holds ADP and phosphate from the ATP it split; it binds actin, then releases them during the power stroke. A head carrying fresh ATP is a detached head.

q: In a working skeletal muscle fibre, ATP is directly needed for which pair of processes?
o: Releasing Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binding Ca²⁺ to troponin
Binding Ca²⁺ to troponin and shifting tropomyosin
Detaching myosin heads and pumping Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Releasing Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion of acetylcholine
x: ATP must bind to release each myosin head from actin, and the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum use ATP. Calcium release, binding to troponin and diffusion are passive.

q: A chemical blocks acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions. The most direct effect is that:
o: No acetylcholine is released from the nerve ending
Acetylcholine stays in the cleft and the fibres are stimulated for too long
The sarcoplasmic reticulum cannot store Ca²⁺
Myosin heads can no longer split ATP
x: With the enzyme blocked, acetylcholine is not broken down, so it keeps acting on the receptors and the muscle stays excited. Release of acetylcholine itself is not affected.

q: A drug blocks the acetylcholine receptors on skeletal muscle fibres. When the motor nerve fires, the muscle will:
o: Fail to contract and stay relaxed
Go into rigor because ATP is used up
x: Acetylcholine is still released but cannot bind, so the sarcolemma is not depolarised and no calcium is released. The muscle is paralysed in a relaxed state, unlike blocking acetylcholinesterase.

q: A muscle fibre has plenty of ATP, but its sarcoplasmic reticulum cannot release Ca²⁺ when stimulated. The fibre will:
o: Not contract, because tropomyosin keeps the actin binding sites covered
Contract continuously, because ATP is plentiful
Go into rigor, because myosin heads cannot detach
Contract normally, because calcium is not needed
x: Without calcium, troponin does not move tropomyosin, so myosin cannot reach actin. ATP alone cannot start contraction, and rigor needs a lack of ATP.

q: A sarcomere shortens from 2.8 µm to 2.2 µm during contraction. Its A band is 1.6 µm long. What is the total I-band length in the contracted sarcomere?
x: The A band does not change, so the I band is the rest of the sarcomere: 2.2 − 1.6 = 0.6 µm in total (0.3 µm on each side). 1.2 µm was the I-band length before contraction.

q: During contraction, the distance between neighbouring Z lines:
x: The thin filaments are anchored to the Z lines, so as they are pulled toward the centre the Z lines come closer and the sarcomere shortens.

q: In a strongly contracted sarcomere the H zone has disappeared completely. This shows that:
o: Thick filaments have shortened until they vanished
Thin filaments from both ends have slid in until they meet at the centre
The A band has shortened to zero length
The I band has become longer
x: The H zone is the part of the A band without thin filaments. It disappears when the thin filaments from both Z lines reach the middle; thick filaments and the A band keep their length.

q: The sutures joining the bones of the skull are:
x: Skull sutures are immovable fibrous joints, where bones are tightly joined by fibrous connective tissue with no joint cavity.

q: The shoulder joint is an example of a:
x: At the shoulder the rounded head of the humerus fits into a cup-shaped socket of the scapula, a ball-and-socket joint allowing movement in all directions.

q: The elbow joint between the humerus and the ulna is a:
x: The elbow lets the forearm bend and straighten in one plane, like a door hinge. Rotation of the forearm happens at a separate pivot joint between the radius and ulna.

q: Ligaments are strong bands of connective tissue that connect:
x: Ligaments join bones to other bones across a joint and hold the joint together. Tendons are the cords that attach muscles to bones.

q: Joints that move freely and have a fluid-filled cavity are called:
x: Synovial joints, such as the knee and shoulder, have a cavity filled with synovial fluid and allow free movement. Fibrous joints and sutures are immovable; cartilaginous joints move only slightly.

q: Shaking the head side to side to say 'no' mainly uses the joint between the atlas and axis vertebrae. This is a:
x: At the atlas–axis joint the atlas rotates around a peg-like projection of the axis, so it is a pivot joint allowing rotation.

q: The joint at the base of the thumb, between a carpal and the first metacarpal, is a:
x: The thumb's carpometacarpal joint is the classic saddle joint: both bone surfaces are saddle-shaped, allowing movement in two planes and opposition of the thumb.

q: The joints between the carpal bones of the wrist are:
x: Neighbouring carpal bones have nearly flat surfaces that slide over one another, so they form gliding (plane) joints. The saddle joint lies at the base of the thumb.

q: Which of the following is an example of a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint?
o: The wrist joint between the radius and carpal bones
The joint between the atlas and axis
x: At the wrist an oval surface of the carpals fits into a hollow of the radius: a condyloid joint allowing movement in two planes. The atlas–axis joint is a pivot and the shoulder is ball-and-socket.

q: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint. It therefore allows:
o: Movement in all planes, including rotation
Bending and straightening in one plane only
x: The ball-shaped head of the femur fits into the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing movement in every direction, including rotation. Movement in one plane only describes a hinge joint.

q: Which pair consists of hinge joints?
o: Base of thumb and joints between carpals
x: The knee and ankle move mainly in one plane, so they are hinge joints. Shoulder and hip are ball-and-socket; atlas–axis is a pivot and the wrist is condyloid.

q: The joint between the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis (pubic symphysis) is a:
x: In the pubic symphysis the bones are joined by a pad of cartilage with no joint cavity. It allows only slight movement, as cartilaginous joints do.

q: The joints between the bodies of neighbouring vertebrae, joined by intervertebral discs, are:
o: Fibrous joints that allow no movement
Cartilaginous joints that allow slight movement
x: Intervertebral discs of cartilage join the vertebral bodies. Each joint moves only a little, but together they make the backbone flexible.

q: The main functions of synovial fluid are to:
o: Produce blood cells for the joint
Lubricate the joint and nourish the articular cartilage
Attach the muscles to the bones
x: Synovial fluid reduces friction between the bone ends and supplies nutrients to the articular cartilage, which has no blood vessels. Binding bones is the job of ligaments.

q: Synovial fluid is secreted by the:
o: Articular cartilage on the bone ends
Synovial membrane lining the joint capsule
x: The synovial membrane lines the inside of the joint capsule and secretes synovial fluid into the joint cavity.

q: In a synovial joint, the ends of the bones are covered with:
x: The bone ends in a synovial joint are capped with smooth hyaline cartilage called articular cartilage, which reduces friction. Elastic cartilage is found in the ear pinna and epiglottis.

q: Which feature is present in synovial joints but absent in fibrous joints?
o: Collagen fibres in the connective tissue
Dense connective tissue around the bones
A joint cavity filled with synovial fluid
x: Only synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity between the bones. Collagen and dense connective tissue occur in both kinds, and serrated edges are a feature of skull sutures.

q: Which match of joint type and mobility is correct?
x: Synovial joints are the freely movable joints. Fibrous joints are immovable and cartilaginous joints allow only slight movement.

q: The joints holding the teeth in their sockets in the jaw bones are:
x: Each tooth is held in its socket by fibrous connective tissue, forming an immovable fibrous joint. There is no cartilage pad or synovial cavity.

q: In a pivot joint, the movement allowed is:
o: Bending and straightening in one plane
Rotation only, of one bone around a single axis
Sliding of flat surfaces over one another
Movement in all planes including circling
x: A pivot joint lets one bone turn around its long axis against another, as at the atlas–axis joint. Bending in one plane is a hinge, and movement in all planes is ball-and-socket.

q: Gliding (plane) joints allow:
o: Rotation of one bone around another
Flat surfaces to slide over one another with limited movement
Bending in one plane like a door hinge
x: In gliding joints the bone surfaces are nearly flat, so they only slide a little on each other. Rotation describes pivot joints and movement in all planes describes ball-and-socket joints.

q: The saddle joint at the base of the thumb allows:
o: Rotation only, like turning a key
Movement in two planes, so the thumb can touch the fingertips
x: The saddle-shaped surfaces allow the thumb to move in two planes; this lets it be brought across the palm to touch each fingertip (opposition).

q: Tendons are made mainly of:
o: Dense connective tissue rich in collagen fibres
x: Tendons are tough cords of dense fibrous connective tissue packed with collagen fibres, which gives them great strength in pulling on bones.

q: The joint capsule of a synovial joint is:
o: A layer of hyaline cartilage covering the bone ends
A pad of fibrocartilage between vertebrae
A sleeve of fibrous tissue enclosing the cavity, lined by synovial membrane
A tendon that attaches a muscle to the joint
x: The capsule wraps around the joint, enclosing the cavity; its inner synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid. Hyaline cartilage covers the bone ends inside the capsule.

q: Which statement about cartilaginous joints is correct?
o: They contain a cavity filled with synovial fluid
The bones are joined by cartilage, with no fluid-filled cavity
They are the most freely movable joints
They join the flat bones of the skull
x: In cartilaginous joints, such as the pubic symphysis, cartilage unites the bones and there is no joint cavity, so movement is slight. Skull bones are joined by fibrous sutures.

q: The joints between the phalanges of the fingers (interphalangeal joints) are:
x: The finger joints only bend and straighten in one plane, so they are hinge joints.

q: Turning the palm up and down involves rotation of the radius against the ulna near the elbow. This joint is a:
x: The head of the radius rotates within a ring against the ulna, making a pivot joint. The hinge joint at the elbow is between the humerus and ulna and only bends and straightens.

q: In a sports injury, a strong band of tissue joining the femur directly to the tibia inside the knee is torn. This band is a:
x: A band linking one bone to another is a ligament. A tendon would connect a muscle to a bone, not femur to tibia.

q: Which list places these joints in order from least movable to most movable?
o: Skull suture → pubic symphysis → shoulder joint
Shoulder joint → pubic symphysis → skull suture
Pubic symphysis → skull suture → shoulder joint
Skull suture → shoulder joint → pubic symphysis
x: A suture is an immovable fibrous joint, the pubic symphysis is a slightly movable cartilaginous joint, and the shoulder is a freely movable synovial joint.

q: Which joint type is INCORRECTLY matched with its example?
o: Gliding — joints between the tarsal bones
x: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, not a pivot; a pivot example is the atlas–axis joint. The other three pairings are correct.

q: The arm can swing in a full circle at the shoulder, but the forearm moves only back and forth at the elbow. This is because:
o: The shoulder is ball-and-socket, moving in all planes; the elbow is a hinge, moving in one
The shoulder is a hinge joint, while the elbow is ball-and-socket
The shoulder is a cartilaginous joint, while the elbow is fibrous
The shoulder has no ligaments, while the elbow has many
x: A ball in a socket allows movement in every direction, so the arm can circle. A hinge lets the forearm move in a single plane only. Both are synovial joints with ligaments.

q: Arthritis is best defined as:
o: Loss of bone mass, making bones brittle
Inflammation of one or more joints
x: Arthritis means inflammation of joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. Loss of bone mass is osteoporosis, a different disorder.

q: Gout is caused by the deposition in joints of crystals of:
x: In gout, a raised level of uric acid in the blood leads to urate crystals forming in the joints, which become inflamed. Urea is a soluble waste that does not form joint crystals.

q: Rheumatoid arthritis is:
o: A result of wear and tear with age
Caused by a lack of vitamin D
x: In rheumatoid arthritis the body's own immune system attacks the joint tissues. Uric acid crystals cause gout, and wear and tear causes osteoarthritis.

q: Osteoarthritis mainly involves:
o: Wearing away of the articular cartilage
An immune attack on the synovial membrane
Loss of calcium from the skull bones
x: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative disease in which the cartilage covering the bone ends gradually wears away. Urate crystals are gout, and immune attack is rheumatoid arthritis.

q: Gout classically first affects the joint at the base of the:
x: The typical first attack of gout is sudden, intense pain and swelling at the base of the big toe.

q: In rheumatoid arthritis, the tissue that first becomes inflamed and thickened is the:
o: Tendon sheath of the toe only
x: Rheumatoid arthritis begins as inflammation of the synovial membrane, which thickens and then damages the cartilage and bone of the joint.

q: Osteoarthritis is most common in:
o: Newborn babies, in the fontanelles of the skull
Teenagers, in the sutures of the skull
Elderly people, in weight-bearing joints such as knees and hips
Young children, in the joints between vertebral bodies
x: Osteoarthritis develops with age as cartilage wears, so it is mainly seen in older people, especially in weight-bearing joints such as the knees and hips.

q: An attack of gout is more likely in a person whose diet is rich in:
o: Red meat and organ meats such as liver
x: Red meat and organ meats are rich in purines, which the body breaks down into uric acid. Raised uric acid favours the urate crystals of gout.

q: Bony outgrowths (spurs) at the edges of a joint are a typical feature of:
x: In osteoarthritis the cartilage wears away and the exposed bone forms bony spurs at the joint margins. Rheumatoid arthritis instead erodes bone, and osteoporosis is a general loss of bone mass.

q: Which feature is typical of rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis?
o: It mainly affects weight-bearing joints of elderly people
The same joints on both sides of the body are affected
It results from wear of the articular cartilage
Bony spurs form at the joint edges
x: Rheumatoid arthritis usually affects joints symmetrically, for example both hands. Wear of cartilage, bony spurs and weight-bearing joints in the elderly are features of osteoarthritis.

q: In advanced cases, the bones of a joint may become fused and immovable in:
x: In rheumatoid arthritis the inflamed synovial membrane destroys cartilage, and the bones may fuse, leaving a stiff, deformed joint. Cramp and tetany are muscle disorders.

q: Which statement about gout is correct?
o: It is linked to raised uric acid in the blood and urate crystals in joints
It is an autoimmune attack on the synovial membrane
It is caused by age-related wear of the cartilage
It is caused by low calcium in the blood
x: Gout is a disorder of uric acid: when the blood level is high, urate crystals deposit in joints and cause painful inflammation. The other statements describe other conditions.

q: The blood uric acid level can rise, leading to gout, if too much uric acid is produced or if the kidneys:
x: Uric acid is removed from the blood by the kidneys. If they excrete too little, it accumulates and may crystallise in joints.

q: A 35-year-old woman has painful, swollen small joints in both hands and feet, with stiffness every morning lasting over an hour. The likely condition is:
x: Symmetrical swelling of small joints in a younger woman with long morning stiffness is typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Osteoarthritis mainly affects older people's weight-bearing joints.

q: A 72-year-old overweight man has knee pain that gets worse after walking. An X-ray shows thinned cartilage and bony spurs. The likely condition is:
x: Thinning of articular cartilage with bony spurs in a weight-bearing joint of an older person is typical of osteoarthritis.

q: A man wakes at night with sudden, very painful, red and swollen joint at the base of his big toe after a large meal of red meat. The likely condition is:
x: A sudden attack at the base of the big toe after a purine-rich meal is typical of gout, caused by urate crystals in the joint.

q: In osteoarthritis, the joint becomes painful mainly because:
o: Urate crystals deposit inside the joint
Bone surfaces rub against each other after the cartilage wears away
The immune system attacks the synovial membrane
x: Once the protective articular cartilage has worn thin, the bone ends grind together, causing pain and stiffness.

q: Which is NOT a feature of osteoarthritis?
o: Bony spurs may form at the joint edges
It is common in elderly people
x: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative wear-and-tear disease, not an autoimmune one. Autoimmune attack on the joint describes rheumatoid arthritis.

q: Which is a recognised risk factor for osteoarthritis of the knee?
o: A low blood uric acid level
x: Extra body weight puts more load on weight-bearing joints such as the knee and speeds the wear of cartilage. Purines and uric acid relate to gout, and osteoarthritis is a disease of older people.

q: Which pairing of a type of arthritis with the tissue it mainly damages is correct?
x: Osteoarthritis is the breakdown of articular cartilage on bone ends. Rheumatoid arthritis starts in the synovial membrane, and gout affects synovial joints such as the big toe.

q: The forms of arthritis studied (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout) mainly affect which type of joint?
x: These diseases damage the articular cartilage, the synovial membrane or the joint cavity, all of which belong to synovial joints such as the knee, hip and big toe.

q: The common symptoms of arthritis are:
o: Loss of feeling in the skin
Pain, swelling and stiffness of the joints
x: Inflamed joints are painful, swollen and stiff, and movement is reduced. Brittle bones describe osteoporosis, and cramps are a muscle problem.

q: Which statement about who is mainly affected is correct?
o: Rheumatoid arthritis is more common in men, while gout is more common in women
Rheumatoid arthritis is more common in women, while gout is more common in men
Both are found only in young children
Osteoarthritis is found mainly in teenagers
x: Rheumatoid arthritis affects women more often than men, while gout is more common in men. Osteoarthritis is mainly a disease of older people.

q: In gout, the deposition of urate crystals in a joint leads to:
o: Sudden attacks of intense pain, redness and swelling
x: Urate crystals trigger acute inflammation, so gout attacks come on suddenly with severe pain, redness and swelling of the joint.

q: Osteoarthritis differs from osteoporosis because osteoarthritis:
o: Is loss of bone mass, while osteoporosis is a joint disease
Is a joint disease with cartilage breakdown, while osteoporosis is loss of bone mass
Is caused by uric acid, while osteoporosis is autoimmune
Affects only children, while osteoporosis affects only adults
x: Osteoarthritis damages the cartilage of joints. Osteoporosis is thinning of bone tissue throughout the skeleton, making bones brittle and easy to fracture.

q: Which of the following disorders is a form of arthritis?
x: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in joints. Osteoporosis and rickets are bone disorders, and tetany is a muscle disorder.

q: A patient's joint fluid contains needle-shaped crystals and his blood uric acid is high. The substance in these crystals comes from the breakdown of:
o: Haem from old red blood cells
x: The crystals of gout are urates. Uric acid is formed by breaking down purine bases of nucleic acids; deamination of amino acids gives urea instead.

q: Which pair of descriptions correctly separates osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Osteoarthritis: immune attack on the synovial membrane; rheumatoid: cartilage wear with age
Osteoarthritis: urate crystals; rheumatoid: cartilage wear with age
Osteoarthritis: immune attack on cartilage; rheumatoid: urate crystals
Osteoarthritis: cartilage wear with age; rheumatoid: immune attack on the synovial membrane
x: Osteoarthritis is degenerative wear of articular cartilage, while rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammation that starts in the synovial membrane. Urate crystals belong to gout.

q: Which statement is true of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout alike?
o: Each damages joints, causing pain and stiffness
Each is caused by urate crystals
x: All three are forms of arthritis that cause painful, stiff joints, but their causes differ: wear, autoimmunity and urate crystals respectively.

q: A woman's immune system is attacking her own joint linings, which are swollen and thickened. If the disease progresses, the joints are likely to show:
o: Erosion of cartilage and bone, with deformity
Bony spurs from cartilage wear only
Complete regrowth of healthy articular cartilage
x: This is rheumatoid arthritis. The inflamed, thickened synovial membrane erodes cartilage and bone, leading to deformed and sometimes fused joints. Urate crystals belong to gout.

q: Which is the correct sequence of changes in osteoarthritis?
o: Bony spurs form → cartilage thins → bone ends rub
Bone ends rub → cartilage thickens → urate crystals form
Synovial membrane inflamed → cartilage thickens → bones fuse
Cartilage thins and cracks → bone ends rub → bony spurs form and joint stiffens
x: Osteoarthritis begins with wear of the articular cartilage. Bone then rubs on bone, and the body forms bony spurs at the margins, making the joint stiff and painful.
